e.etymology: A name with several sources: an elaboration of Welsh Sian, the form of Jane ('God is gracious'); the Bulgarian name Siyana; and in the US often a variant of Sianna or Sienna.
From Arabic yasir, 'easy, well-off', from the root for ease and prosperity. Yasir ibn Amir was an early companion of Muhammad.
The Hebrew form of Reuben, Jacob's eldest son in Genesis, traditionally read as re'u ben, 'see, a son'. In the US it is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish families.
A spelling of Johanna that writes the opening Y sound of the Hebrew original, Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. Spanish-speaking families use it alongside Yohana and Johana.
In French, Maélie is an elaboration of Maëlle, the feminine of Breton Maël, 'chief, prince', used in Quebec and France. Americans often read it as Mae with the -lie ending of Rosalie.
The Hawaiian word 'ohana, 'family' in the wide sense of kin and close community. Disney's Lilo & Stitch made it familiar with the line 'Ohana means family'.

assoc.t: 'Ohana means family', the line from Lilo & Stitch

e.meaning: pet form of Tatiana, of the Roman family Tatius
e.etymology: Russian pet form of Tatiana, the name of a 3rd-century Roman martyr, from the Roman family name Tatius. English speakers borrowed Tanya in the 20th century, and it peaked in the 1970s.
namesakes: Tanya Roberts (actress, Charlie's Angels and A View to a Kill)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jody, which grew out of Judy, the pet form of Judith, Hebrew for 'woman of Judea'. For boys, Jody has been a pet form of Joseph and Jude.
namesakes: Jodi Benson (voice of Ariel in The Little Mermaid)

e.etymology: A spelling of Ricky or Ricki, pet forms of Richard for boys and of Erica and Frederica for girls. All contain the Germanic element ric, 'ruler, power'.

assoc.t: Steely Dan's 1974 hit Rikki Don't Lose That Number

e.etymology: From the English word marvel, 'a wonder', from Old French merveille and Latin mirabilia, 'wonderful things'; also an English surname. It had its first run as a name around 1900, long before the comics.

assoc.t: Marvel, the superhero comics and film studio

e.etymology: Pet form of Joan, the medieval English form of Johanna, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.

assoc.t: Joanie Cunningham of Happy Days and Joanie Loves Chachi

e.etymology: A surname, in Ireland from Ó hAilche, best known from astronomer Edmond Halley and his comet. Use for girls peaked in 1986, the year Halley's Comet last passed; it also resembles Hailey and Hallie.

assoc.t: Halley's Comet, seen from Earth about every 76 years

e.etymology: From Aramaic talitha, 'little girl'. In Mark 5:41 Jesus raises a child with the words Talitha cumi, 'Little girl, arise', and the first word became a given name.
Russian form of Andrew, from Greek Andreas, related to andreios, 'manly', and aner, 'man'. St. Andrew the apostle is a patron saint of Russia.
A respelling of Fallon, an Irish surname from Ó Fallamhain, 'descendant of Fallamhan', a personal name meaning leader. Fallon became a girls' name through Fallon Carrington on the 1980s soap Dynasty.

assoc.t: sounds like Fallon: Tonight Show host Jimmy Fallon (surname)

e.etymology: From the Mediterranean island, Italy's largest, named for the Sicels, a people who lived there before the Greeks came. As a first name it also overlaps with Cicely, an old English form of Cecilia.

assoc.t: Italian island off the toe of the boot

e.etymology: Usually taken from Arabic khalila, 'close friend, beloved', the feminine of Khalil. Kalila is also a jackal in Kalila wa Dimna, the classic Arabic book of animal fables.

e.meaning: joyful, content; in Persian, a sapling
e.etymology: From Persian nihal, 'sapling, young shoot', the sense kept in the Turkish girls' name. In Hindi, Urdu and Punjabi the word came to mean flourishing, happy and content, which is how the Indian boys' name is understood.
A respelling of Lyric, the English word for the words of a song, from Greek lyrikos, 'sung to the lyre'.
From Sanskrit ahana, a Vedic word for the dawn; the doubled a marks a long first vowel. Indian parents often gloss it as the first rays of the sun.

e.meaning: round, stout (old name Cada); or barrel maker
e.etymology: A respelling of Cade, an English surname with several medieval sources, among them the Old English personal name Cada and a trade name for a barrel maker.

e.meaning: mythical bird reborn from its ashes
e.etymology: A simplified spelling of Phoenix, from Greek phoinix, the mythical bird that burns and rises renewed from its ashes; the word also meant crimson. Phénix is the French spelling.

assoc.t: the phoenix, mythical firebird reborn from ashes

e.etymology: A respelling of Prince, the royal title, from Old French prince and Latin princeps, 'first, chief'.

assoc.t: sounds like Prince, the Purple Rain musician

e.etymology: Used as a phonetic spelling of Wren, the songbird, and as a short form of Renee, Lauren or Warren. Renn is also an English and German surname.

assoc.t: Kylo Ren of Star Wars (spelled Ren)

e.etymology: A modern compound of May and Lee, more often spelled Maylee. It sounds like the Chinese name Meili, 'beautiful'.
A modern Arabic girls' name. Arabic name guides usually explain it as 'young gazelle', from Turkish maral, while Rula Jebreal's novel Miral describes it as a red roadside flower.
Danish and Norwegian surname meaning son of Ole, the everyday form of Olaf, from Old Norse Aleifr, 'ancestor's heir'.

assoc.t: the Olsen sisters: Mary-Kate, Ashley and Elizabeth

e.etymology: A recent American coinage, also spelled Jakari, in the family of Jakobi, Zakari and Jahmari. The Jah- spelling echoes Jah, the Rastafarian name for God.
A recent coinage that crosses Maeve, the Irish queen's name meaning 'intoxicating', with Maven, the Yiddish-derived word for an expert.
Its origin as a first name is not established. The same spelling is a Japanese surname, and it is close in form to Asa, Isai and Asaiah.
A stylized spelling of the English word dream, with Jh- standing in for the Dr- sound, as in the related spelling Jream.
A spelling of Hayley, an English surname from a place name: Old English heg, 'hay', and leah, 'clearing, meadow'. Actress Hayley Mills made it familiar as a girls' name in the 1960s.
namesakes: Haylie Duff (actress, sister of Hilary Duff)
